stem: Which of the following are considered minimum functional components of a complete agentic loop? (Select 2)

options.text: A reasoning core that decides what action to take
A termination condition that determines when to stop
A long-term memory database
A planning module that creates multi-step plans in advance

explanation.why_correct: A reasoning core and a termination condition are both part of the strictly minimal agent loop -- without a decision-maker there is no agency, and without a stopping condition the loop would never end.

why_incorrect.C: Long-term memory is a common enhancement but not a strict requirement -- a reactive agent can operate within a single task with no persistent memory across sessions.
why_incorrect.D: Explicit upfront planning is one strategy among several for sequencing actions, but reactive agents can decide one action at a time without a separate planning module.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The strictly minimal agent loop needs a decision-maker and a stopping condition; memory and explicit planning are valuable but optional enhancements.

stem: Which of the following are genuine limitations of a single-shot LLM call that agentic designs are intended to address? (Select 2)

options.text: Inability to access information outside its training data and prompt context
Inability to verify or revise its own output before it is finalized
Inability to generate grammatically correct sentences
Inability to process more than one word at a time

explanation.why_correct: A single-shot call cannot fetch live or external data beyond its training and prompt, and it has no built-in step to check its own answer -- both are real gaps that tool use and self-critique/reflection loops respectively address.

why_incorrect.C: Modern LLMs are generally capable of producing grammatically correct text in a single pass; this is not the limitation agentic designs target.
why_incorrect.D: LLMs process input as sequences of tokens with full context, not strictly one word at a time in the sense implied; this is not a genuine limitation driving agentic design.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The real motivations for agentic design are grounding (fresh/external knowledge) and self-correction (verification/revision) -- not basic language fluency, which single-shot calls already handle well.

stem: Which of the following systems should be classified as workflows rather than agents? (Select 2)

options.text: A system that always runs steps A, then B, then C, in that fixed order, regardless of input
A system that classifies input into one of five predefined branches using a fixed classifier, with no further runtime decisions
A system where the model decides, at runtime, which of an open-ended set of tools to call and how many times
A system where the model decides when to stop iterating based on its own assessment of task completion

explanation.why_correct: Both a fixed sequential pipeline and a fixed-branch classifier represent control flow fully authored in advance by a developer, with no runtime decision-making by the model about what to do next -- the defining trait of a workflow.

why_incorrect.C: Dynamically choosing among an open-ended set of tools at runtime is exactly the kind of model-driven decision-making that characterizes an agent, not a workflow.
why_incorrect.D: Deciding when to stop based on the model's own assessment (rather than a fixed step count defined in advance) is an agentic trait, since the termination point is determined dynamically.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Fixed sequences and fixed-branch classifiers are workflows; dynamic tool selection and model-decided termination are hallmarks of agentic control flow.

stem: Which of the following are legitimate reasons to deliberately LIMIT an agent's autonomy rather than maximizing it? (Select 2)

options.text: The task involves actions that are costly or impossible to reverse if done incorrectly
The system needs to be predictable and auditable for compliance reasons
Full autonomy is always technically impossible to implement
Limiting autonomy guarantees the agent will never make mistakes

explanation.why_correct: High-stakes, hard-to-reverse actions and the need for predictable, auditable behavior are both well-established, legitimate engineering reasons to constrain an agent's autonomy rather than maximizing it.

why_incorrect.C: Full autonomy is technically achievable in many systems; the reasons to limit it are about risk and predictability tradeoffs, not technical impossibility.
why_incorrect.D: Limiting autonomy reduces risk surface and improves predictability, but it does not guarantee error-free behavior -- a constrained agent can still make mistakes within its narrower scope.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Autonomy limits are a deliberate risk/predictability tradeoff, driven by the cost of errors and auditability needs -- not a technical limitation or an error-elimination guarantee.

stem: Which of the following properties are commonly used to characterize an AI agent? (Select 2)

options.text: Some degree of autonomy in deciding its own next action
Goal-directed behavior organized toward an objective
Guaranteed perfect accuracy on every task
A requirement to always use at least three different tools per task

explanation.why_correct: Autonomy over deciding next actions and goal-directedness are the two core properties most commonly used to characterize what makes a system agentic, as opposed to a fixed function or script.

why_incorrect.C: No accuracy guarantee is implied by or required for a system to be considered an agent; agents can and do make mistakes while still being agentic.
why_incorrect.D: There is no fixed minimum tool-count requirement for agency; a minimal agent could use zero or one tool depending on the task.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Agency is characterized by autonomy and goal-directedness, not by any guarantee of accuracy or a fixed tool-usage quota.
